title: FAST '26 - ScaleSwap: A Scalable OS Swap System for All-Flash Swap Arrays
transcriptText:
I'm Chanyoung You from Chung-Ang
University.
Today, I'll talk about ScaleSwap.
ScaleSwap is a scalable swap system
designed to use all flash swap arrays
efficiently.
This work is a collaboration with Taewan
Um and Sangji Lee from Chung-Ang
University and my advisor Yong-Seok Son.
First, let me explain the motivation.
Today, many workloads need a lot of
memory like machine learning, big data,
graph processing.
But, DRAM is expensive and it is hard to
scale DRAM to very large sizes.
So, the total cost becomes high.
At the same time, NVMe SSDs are much
faster now.
So, we can use SSDs as swap space to
extend memory, especially when we have
multiple SSDs.
However, the default Linux swap has a
big problem.
It does not scale well when we use many
CPU cores and many SSDs.
Even with multiple SSDs, Linux swap
still has many shared locks.
So, many cores spend time waiting
instead of doing real work.
That's why SSD performance can scale,
but Linux swap throughput stays almost
flat around 4 GB per second.
So, our main issue is the swap design in
the OS.
Before our design, let me quickly review
Linux page eviction.
Linux uses LRU lists to choose pages to
evict.
There are two lists, active and
inactive.
Active pages are hot, so Linux tries to
keep them.
And inactive pages are cold, so Linux uh
checks them first.
When memory pressure happens,
Linux scans the inactive list.
If a page was used again, it can move
back to active.
If not, it becomes a victim for reclaim
or swap out.
This slide shows the basic flow under
memory pressure.
When a process needs a new pages,
uh new page, it first tries to allocate
one.
If there is uh
free page, allocation is simple.
But, if there is no free page, Linux
must reclaim memory.
It scans inactive LRU list, select a
victim, and evict out.
Then, Linux can get a free page and
continue.
The important point is uh many threads
can do the can do this at the same time,
so lock overhead can become a problem.
Now, let's move to swap.
Swap uses uh storage space as memory
when DRAM is not enough.
For swap out, Linux evicts a victim page
to the swap area and changes the page
table entry from page table entry to
swap entry.
For swapping, when the process touches
that page again, Linux gets a page
fault. Then, Linux reads the page from
the swap area and restores the entry
from swap entry back to page table
entry.
This slide shows a simple swap flow.
During swap out, Linux picks a victim
page from the inactive list, updates
swap metadata with spin lock, writes the
page to SSD, and updates the page page
table entry to swap entry.
During swap in,
it sees swap entry on a page fault,
finds the swap slot, and updates swap
metadata with spin lock,
loads the page back to memory and put
put it back into the LRU list.
So, swap is not only IO, we also touch
swap metadata many times.
Now, let's talk about the first
bottleneck.
The first bottleneck is lock contention
on the LRU list.
Linux manages LRU list per node and many
cores share the same LRU lock.
When memory pressure is high, many
threads try to reclaim at the same time.
So, cores spend a lot of time waiting
for the LRU lock.
This reduces throughput even if the SSDs
are fast.
The second bottleneck is lock contention
on swap metadata.
Swap in and swap out both update
metadata like the swap map.
Uh in Linux, this metadata is protected
by a swap
swap metadata lock. So, when many cores
swap at the same time, the lock becomes
very hot.
This is one main reason why Linux swap
throughput stops scaling.
So, our goal is to make swap scale well
with more cores and more SSDs,
especially for all flash swap arrays.
And to do that, our key idea is to avoid
a centralized design.
Instead, we use a decentralized
core-centric design.
We use three strategies.
First, core-centric swap resource
management. Second, opportunistic
inter-core swap assistance using
delegation.
Third, core affinity page and LRU
management.
This slide shows the overall structure
of ScaleSwap.
Swap resources are no longer global
shared.
They are owned by individual cores.
Each core has its own swap resources
such as swap metadata, swap cache, task
queue, and LRU list.
Also, each core has a delegator thread.
When a core needs help from another
core's swap resources, it sends a task
to that core's delegator.
This way, we reduce global sharing and
improve scalability.
Here,
uh we compare how Linux and ScaleSwap
manage swap resources.
In Linux, swap allocation depends on a
global view and shared work, so many
cores can touch the same
uh swap metadata.
But, in ScaleSwap, we use a core-centric
design. Uh each core owns its own swap
space and metadata.
So, most swap operations stay local and
we reduce
contention.
As a result, allocation no longer
requires global co-coordination.
A core can allocate directly from its
local swap region
instead of touching global lists.
However, this ownership model raises a
question.
What if a core's local swap space is
full?
Or what if we need to access swap
metadata owned by another core?
To handle this, we use delegation.
Instead of touching remote metadata
directly, we send a task to the target
core's delegator.
One important point is the application
thread still does the real IO, so we
keep SSD parallel parallelism.
Now, I'll explain what happens during
delegation.
For swap out,
if local swap space is full, the
requester picks a victim page.
Then, the requester asks another core to
handle the swap out metadata work.
The delegator updates the swap entry and
related metadata,
and the requester updates page table
entry to swap entry.
For swapping,
on a page fault, we first check the swap
cache.
If it's a hit, we read from cache if but
if not, we read from the uh swap space.
The requesters restores page table entry
and puts the back puts the page into the
local LRU list.
Then, the delegator updates the swap
metadata asynchronously.
The next design component is core
affinity page LRU uh page and LRU
management.
In Linux,
LRU lists are shared per NUMA node, so
many cores contend on the same LRU lock
under memory pressure.
To minimize this this contention, we
partition LRU lists by core, removing
shared LRU locking.
In addition, we modify the page flag
layout to store the allocation CPU ID.
This ensures that when a page is swapped
in or out, it returns to the original
core's LRU list.
Together, this design minimizes lock
contention and improves locality.
Now, I'll move to evaluation.
We evaluate ScaleSwap on a multi-core
system equipped with multiple NVMe SSDs
to study scalability.
We run microbenchmarks and real-world
applications and compare ScaleSwap
against Linux swap, TMO, and EXT4.
On this slide, I show the micro
benchmark results in terms of throughput
and latency.
Scale swap scales almost linearly as we
increase the number of SSDs and cores,
while Linux swap saturates only due to
lock contention.
Overall, Scale swap achieves up to 3.4
times higher throughput compared to
Linux swap.
In terms of latency,
Scale swap remains stable without large
spikes even under heavy memory pressure.
It achieves up to 11.5
times lower average latency,
indicating significantly reduced
synchronization overhead.
Now, I show results from real-world
applications.
We evaluate five memory-intensive
workloads, including BFS and DNA
visualization.
With eight SSDs,
Scale swap consistently outperforms
Linux swap across all workloads.
For example, BFS improved throughput by
2.4 times and DNA visualization by
2.57 times.
The other workloads also show consistent
improvements.
This shows that the benefit extends
beyond micro benchmarks to real
applications.
This slide shows results from Apache
Spark.
Spark runs many parallel tasks and
generates high memory pressure.
We use PySpark with the Common Crawl
dataset, which requires terabytes of
memory and heavily stresses swap.
Scale swap reaches about 6.3 GB/s peak
throughput and achieves 1.75 times
higher throughput than Linux swap.
Here, we compare Scale swap with TMO and
EXT4 mem.
For TMO, the main issue is CPU overhead.
TMO uses compression and decompression,
so CPU cost can be high.
In contrast, Scale swap directly utilize
raw NVMe bandwidth without compression.
For EXT4 mem,
the key limitation is its limited
scalability under increasing SSD and
thread counts.
As the number of SSDs increases,
EXT4 mem shows little performance
improvement and its throughput saturates
beyond 32 threads.
In contrast, Scale swap continues to
scale consistently with both additional
SSDs and higher
thread counts.
As a result, in this all-flash setting,
Scale swap achieves up to 1.64 higher
performance than TMO and 5.02 times
higher throughput than EXT4 mem.
To conclude,
Scale swap is a swap system designed for
all-flash swap arrays.
We redesigned swap to scale with
increasing numbers of cores and SSDs.
We achieve this through three key design
choices.
First, swap resources are owned by
individual cores, eliminating global
lock contention.
Second, remote metadata accesses handled
through delegation, preserving
scalability without sacrificing
parallelism.
Third, core affinity
reduces synchronization overhead and
improves locality.
As a result, Scale swap achieves
significantly higher throughput and much
lower latency than Linux swap,
especially under memory pressure.
We are pleased to announce that Scale
swap is now open source. You can access
it at the URL on the slide.
That concludes my talk. Thank you. Thank
you for your attention.
